belief.text: Building models placed in tombs could provide for an afterlife; elite hopes are especially visible.

production.text: Models depict granaries, wells and animal pens, making estate provisioning visible without representing every household.

authority.text: Earlier Han court arguments connect government with grain, state revenue and frontier demands. These dated texts illuminate institutions without proving unchanged practice in Eastern Han.

evidence.text: Tomb models show selective provision for an afterlife. Earlier memorials and debates show proposals and disputes; neither source type is a census of households.

question: Why put a building in a tomb?
summary: A clay tower is an entry into an imperial society sustained by fields, stored grain, households and officials. Eastern Han rulers governed from Luoyang, but the models buried with wealthy people show a different scale of organization: the estate. Read them beside earlier arguments about revenue and farming to see how political power depended on resources—and how differently an owner and a government adviser could describe the same world.

sections.title: The model is not the building
sections.text: The glazed tower’s roofs, platforms and openings invite close observation. Yet this is pottery made for a tomb, not a reduced photograph of a house. Its broad museum date spans the first through early third century CE. The funerary setting links the object to hopes for continued provision after death. It may also express the standing of the household that commissioned it. Those two readings can coexist: an object can take part in a religious practice while presenting a desirable social world.

sections.title: An estate is a network of work
sections.text: Look beyond the tower to the granary and well. Joanne Pillsbury’s account of architectural models connects such objects with agricultural estates and provision for their owners. Storage links one harvest to later meals; a well makes water available; buildings require materials and upkeep. These are relationships we can investigate through the ensemble, rather than assume from a single imposing tower. The burial record is selective. It makes an owner’s wishes especially visible while rarely naming the people whose routine work sustained those comforts.

sections.title: A court needs food as well as obedience
sections.text: Earlier Han advisers connected rural production with the resources of government. In a memorial dated 178 BCE, Chao Cuo urged the ruler to reward grain deliveries with rank or relief from penalties. His reasoning joined status, stored supplies and frontier needs. This is a policy proposal from Western Han, centuries before many of the featured models. It does not describe the rules on a particular Eastern Han estate. It does reveal a problem that a tomb model cannot answer alone: how could the state persuade or compel resources to move beyond a household?

sections.title: Rule could be argued over
sections.text: A record of the court debate in 81 BCE places two positions side by side. Scholars criticized state monopolies as a pursuit of profit that harmed proper government and farming. The imperial secretary defended revenue as necessary to support frontier protection. Neither position is a neutral account of all livelihoods. Both turn material resources into an argument about legitimate rule. Together they make Han government more intelligible than an image of an emperor simply issuing commands: officials disagreed about means, costs and moral purposes.

sections.title: A later capital in a connected world
sections.text: Eastern Han rule, conventionally dated 25–220 CE, centered on Luoyang after an earlier western phase and an interruption under Wang Mang. Court histories and museum scholarship place the dynasty within wider diplomatic and trading networks. The clay tower does not establish that its owner travelled those routes. Keep three scales in view: a burial object, the household world it evokes, and the political institutions that shaped resource demands. A change at one scale need not transform all the others immediately.

familyActivity.title: Keep an estate working
steps: Find the tower, granary and well using the object choices.
For each model, name something a real household would need: food, water, materials, maintenance or labor.
Choose one need that the model makes visible and one person or task it leaves out.
familyActivity.explanation: A tower draws attention to security and status, but an estate also needs food and water. The models are burial provisions, not a full inventory of a working farm or every family’s home.

deeperReading.title: Whose judgment about farmers?
deeperReading.text: Chao Cuo contrasts hard-pressed farmers with prosperous merchants and proposes that state rewards should make grain more valuable. Treat that contrast as persuasion by an official addressing a ruler. It is evidence of what he wanted policy to do, not a representative survey of merchants’ or farmers’ experiences. His argument can guide a new question: who was able to deliver a surplus and obtain the rewards? The memorial by itself cannot establish the answer for every household.

deeperReading.title: Why use an earlier debate?
deeperReading.text: The salt and iron discussion predates Eastern Han. It belongs here as an explicitly earlier example of how officials linked revenue, the frontier and moral authority. It should not be used to assert that the same monopoly arrangements continued unchanged in 200 CE. The record is also a composed text transmitted through later editions and a modern translation. To read it well, identify the speaker, the policy defended, the audience and the burdens each side emphasizes.

deeperReading.title: Rome and Han: similar problems, different evidence
deeperReading.text: Both investigations connect concentrated power to the work of many people. Their surviving objects answer different questions: the Roman portraits foreground a named identity, while the Han building models foreground provision and a desirable household environment. The distinction is about this selection of evidence, not everything either society produced. A fair comparison keeps the questions constant while allowing the answers and uncertainties to differ. Similarity also establishes no direct contact between these particular objects or owners.

evidenceReading.title: Separate object, proposal and debate
evidenceReading.introduction: The short readings below paraphrase sources; each has its own date and purpose.

items.label: The tower: Eastern Han
items.text: A pottery building was placed in a burial setting.
items.interpretation: Religious provision and household status are useful questions. It is not a government document or a scale survey of a real estate.

items.label: The memorial: 178 BCE
items.text: Chao Cuo proposes rewards for supplying grain.
items.interpretation: An official is recommending an intervention. Ask who could benefit, rather than treating the recommendation as proof that the outcome occurred everywhere.

items.label: The debate: 81 BCE
items.text: Critics emphasize moral government and farming; the official defending monopolies emphasizes the cost of frontier security.
items.interpretation: The disagreement exposes a tradeoff. Neither speaker should be mistaken for the voice of the entire population.
